reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / ECMM-ISHAM guidance
clinicalPearls: A group of infections caused by dematiaceous (darkly pigmented, melanised) fungi such as Cladophialophora, Exophiala, Alternaria, Bipolaris, and Curvularia found in soil and plant matter worldwide
The defining feature is the presence of melanin in the fungal cell wall, giving pigmented hyphae in tissue that can be highlighted with a Fontana-Masson stain
Clinical spectrum ranges from subcutaneous nodules and cysts after traumatic inoculation to allergic fungal sinusitis, keratitis, and life-threatening cerebral abscesses
Cerebral phaeohyphomycosis, notably due to Cladophialophora bantiana, is striking because it can cause brain abscesses in apparently immunocompetent hosts and carries high mortality
Immunosuppressed patients, including transplant recipients, are at risk of disseminated and invasive disease
Management combines surgical excision or drainage with azole-based antifungal therapy, often prolonged, and outcomes for cerebral disease remain poor even with treatment
Diagnosis rests on biopsy with histology showing pigmented hyphae, fungal culture, and molecular identification, since species determines prognosis and drug selection
reference.pathophysiology: Phaeohyphomycosis is caused by melanised moulds acquired mainly through traumatic inoculation of contaminated soil or plant material into skin and subcutaneous tissue, or by inhalation leading to sinus and, rarely, cerebral disease. Melanin in the fungal cell wall is a virulence factor that scavenges free radicals and blunts host defences, contributing to the neurotropism of certain species. Localised disease produces subcutaneous cysts and nodules, whereas neurotropic species such as Cladophialophora bantiana can reach the brain and form abscesses even without evident immunosuppression; in immunocompromised hosts the fungi may invade tissue and disseminate more widely.
additionalDifferentials: Chromoblastomycosis (also caused by dematiaceous fungi but with distinct sclerotic bodies)
Invasive aspergillosis or other hyaline mould infection
Epidermoid or other benign subcutaneous cysts
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy for histopathology, including Fontana-Masson stain to demonstrate melanised hyphae
Fungal culture with molecular species identification
Antifungal susceptibility testing to guide therapy
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain for suspected cerebral abscess
Computed tomography of the sinuses in suspected fungal sinusitis
Assessment of immune status in disseminated or invasive disease
redFlags: New focal neurological signs or a brain abscess on imaging
Disseminated disease in an immunocompromised host
Rapidly enlarging or invasive sinus disease
Isolation of a known neurotropic species such as Cladophialophora bantiana
Progressive lesions despite antifungal therapy, indicating the need for surgical intervention
reference.prognosis: Localised subcutaneous disease often responds well to excision and antifungal therapy, but cerebral phaeohyphomycosis carries a high mortality even with combined surgical and medical treatment, and disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts also has a poor outlook.
pitfalls: Failing to request a melanin stain, so pigmented hyphae are overlooked on histology
Assuming cerebral abscess requires immunosuppression and dismissing it in an immunocompetent patient
Relying on antifungals alone when surgical excision or drainage is often essential
Not obtaining species identification, which strongly influences prognosis and drug choice
Confusing it with chromoblastomycosis or other subcutaneous mycoses that require different management
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ECMM-ISHAM global guideline for the diagnosis and management of rare mould infections
